claims.source: In the chick spinal cord, apical abscission is preceded by dis-assembly of the primary cilium (Das and Storey, 2014) and loss and or retraction of ciliary membrane is also associated with delaminating zebrafish retinal neuroblasts (Lepanto et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Mediators of the mitogenic Sonic hedgehog pathway are processed into activated forms in the primary cilium.
claims.source: Mediators of the mitogenic Sonic hedgehog pathway are processed into activated forms in the primary cilium (Guemez-Gamboa et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2009) and so this may be a further way in which cell biological mechanisms associated with delamination link this process to cell state change.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Following cilium disassembly, the centrosome is retained in the withdrawing neuronal cell process while ciliary and apical membrane are shed.
claims.source: Following cilium disassembly, the centrosome is retained in the withdrawing neuronal cell process while ciliary and apical membrane are shed (Das and Storey, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: Centrosome retention is critical for neuronal migration to form the cortical plate.
claims.source: Centrosome retention is then critical for subsequent neuronal differentiation: for neuronal migration to form the cortical plate (Higginbotham and Gleeson, 2007; Tsai and Gleeson, 2005; Xie et al., 2003), as a microtubule organising centre during axonogenesis (de Anda et al., 2005; Zmuda and Rivas, 1998), and in defining where dendrites will elongate (Puram and Bonni, 2013; Puram et al., 2011), although this is context dependent (Kuijpers and Hoogenraad, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The centrosome acts as a microtubule organising centre during axonogenesis.
claims.source: Centrosome retention is then critical for subsequent neuronal differentiation: for neuronal migration to form the cortical plate (Higginbotham and Gleeson, 2007; Tsai and Gleeson, 2005; Xie et al., 2003), as a microtubule organising centre during axonogenesis (de Anda et al., 2005; Zmuda and Rivas, 1998), and in defining where dendrites will elongate (Puram and Bonni, 2013; Puram et al., 2011), although this is context dependent (Kuijpers and Hoogenraad, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The centrosome is involved in defining where dendrites will elongate.
claims.source: Centrosome retention is then critical for subsequent neuronal differentiation: for neuronal migration to form the cortical plate (Higginbotham and Gleeson, 2007; Tsai and Gleeson, 2005; Xie et al., 2003), as a microtubule organising centre during axonogenesis (de Anda et al., 2005; Zmuda and Rivas, 1998), and in defining where dendrites will elongate (Puram and Bonni, 2013; Puram et al., 2011), although this is context dependent (Kuijpers and Hoogenraad, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature, with a caveat that it is context dependent.

claims.claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton was enriched apically and overlapped with the actin cable and the AJs.
claims.source: The microtubule cytoskeleton was enriched apically and overlapped with the actin cable and the AJs (Figure 1A–A'''').
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunocytochemistry in sections of chick spinal cord.

claims.claim: A sub-apical ring-like microtubule structure exists in neuroepithelial cell apical end-feet with a diameter of 2.57 ± 0.5 μm.
claims.source: Closer examination of microtubule architecture in neuroepithelial cell apical end-feet using en face imaging, revealed a sub-apical ring-like structure (2.57 ± 0.5 μm in diameter, 21 cells, in 2 explants from 2 embryos) and associated microtubules radiating from the centrosome of the primary cilium, identified by γ-tubulin and IFT88, respectively (Figure 1B–B'', C–C' and D–D').
claims.evidence: This is based on measurements from en face imaging.

claims.claim: Microtubules radiate from the centrosome of the primary cilium in neuroepithelial cell apical end-feet.
claims.source: Closer examination of microtubule architecture in neuroepithelial cell apical end-feet using en face imaging, revealed a sub-apical ring-like structure (2.57 ± 0.5 μm in diameter, 21 cells, in 2 explants from 2 embryos) and associated microtubules radiating from the centrosome of the primary cilium, identified by γ-tubulin and IFT88, respectively (Figure 1B–B'', C–C' and D–D').
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by en face imaging with markers for the centrosome and cilium.

claims.claim: A similar microtubule configuration was observed in E12.5 mouse spinal cord and cortex.
claims.source: A similar microtubule configuration was observed by en face imaging of the ventricular surface in E12.5 mouse spinal cord and cortex (Figure 1E, in 4 explants from 2 embryos) indicating conservation of this apical microtubule architecture across species and different regions of the central nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by en face imaging of mouse tissue.

claims.claim: The apical microtubule architecture is conserved across species and different regions of the central nervous system.
claims.source: A similar microtubule configuration was observed by en face imaging of the ventricular surface in E12.5 mouse spinal cord and cortex (Figure 1E, in 4 explants from 2 embryos) indicating conservation of this apical microtubule architecture across species and different regions of the central nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from observations in both chick and mouse tissue.

claims.claim: Actin-tubulin co-alignment was observed in the majority of cells (71%).
claims.source: The alignment of actin and tubulin was then measured at the Z-level defined by N-Cadherin localisation; this revealed actin-tubulin co-alignment in the majority of cells (71%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, 31 cells in 3 explants from 3 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is based on measurements from 3D imaging.

claims.claim: A subset of microtubules extends basal to the actin/N-cadherin junctional region deep into the cell-process.
claims.source: A subset of microtubules was also observed to extend basal to the actin/N-cadherin junctional region deep into the cell-process (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3D imaging.

claims.claim: Radial microtubules emanate in an evenly spaced fashion from the centrosome of the primary cilium in the end-foot.
claims.source: Tracking the trajectory of EB3-GFP comets revealed that radial microtubules emanate in an evenly spaced fashion from the centrosome of the primary cilium in the end-foot (Figure 2A; Figure 2—video 1, 51 cells in 3 explants from 3 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live tissue imaging tracking EB3-GFP comets.

claims.claim: Some EB3-GFP comets run along the actin cable.
claims.source: By combining EB3-GFP and F-tractin-mKate2 to monitor the relationship between these microtubules and the actin cable, we further observed some EB3-GFP comets running along the actin cable (Figure 2B; Figure 2—video 2, 95 cells in 4 explants from 4 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live tissue imaging with dual markers.

claims.claim: Polymerising microtubules are closely aligned with the actin belt.
claims.source: To quantify this relationship, we followed the 2D trajectories of EB3-GFP comets and measured the EB3-GFP/F-tractin-mKate2 inter-peak distance over time. This analysis indicated a close alignment of polymerising microtubules with the actin belt (Figure 2D–F; Figure 2—video 3; trail tracking: 10 cells in 3 explants from 3 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claims.claim: Radial microtubules bend as they reach the periphery and turn to run along the actin cable.
claims.source: Tracking comet movements also delineated microtubule shapes and revealed that radial microtubules bend as they reach the periphery and turn to run along the actin cable (Figure 2C; Figure 2—video 4, 12 cells in 4 explants from 4 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by tracking EB3-GFP comets in live imaging.

claims.claim: Nocodazole treatment for 1 hr depleted apical microtubules.
claims.source: To test the regulatory relationships between apical microtubules, actin and AJs, we next assessed the consequences of microtubule depolymerisation following exposure to Nocodazole for 1 hr. This treatment depleted apical microtubules as expected (Figure 3A, B) and reduced N-Cadherin at AJs (Figure 3A', B') quantified by fluorescence intensity measurements (Figure 3C, C').
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence following drug treatment.

claims.claim: Nocodazole treatment reduced N-Cadherin at AJs.
claims.source: This treatment depleted apical microtubules as expected (Figure 3A, B) and reduced N-Cadherin at AJs (Figure 3A', B') quantified by fluorescence intensity measurements (Figure 3C, C').
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and quantification following drug treatment.

claims.claim: Depletion of microtubules increased distribution of actin within the cell.
claims.source: Depletion of microtubules also increased distribution of actin within the cell (Figure 3A", B", D), however, this did not significantly alter actin levels at the adhesion belt (Figure 3D, D') nor reduce apical end-foot area (Figure 3A''', B''', E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence following nocodazole treatment.

claims.claim: Depletion of microtubules did not significantly alter actin levels at the adhesion belt.
claims.source: Depletion of microtubules also increased distribution of actin within the cell (Figure 3A", B", D), however, this did not significantly alter actin levels at the adhesion belt (Figure 3D, D') nor reduce apical end-foot area (Figure 3A''', B''', E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: Depletion of microtubules did not reduce apical end-foot area.
claims.source: Depletion of microtubules also increased distribution of actin within the cell (Figure 3A", B", D), however, this did not significantly alter actin levels at the adhesion belt (Figure 3D, D') nor reduce apical end-foot area (Figure 3A''', B''', E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of end-foot area measurements.

claims.claim: Brief exposure (15 mins) to Latrunculin-A dramatically reduced apical actin.
claims.source: We next tested the effects of actin depletion on AJs and apical microtubules. Brief exposure (15 mins) to Latrunculin-A which binds actin monomers and so prevents their polymerisation (Coué et al., 1987) dramatically reduced apical actin as expected (Figure 3F, G, H, H').
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence following drug treatment.

claims.claim: Latrunculin-A treatment depleted apical microtubules.
claims.source: This treatment depleted apical microtubules (Figure 3F", G", J) and consistent with this also reduced N-Cadherin at AJs (Figure 3F', G') and quantified in Figure 3I, I'.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and quantification following drug treatment.

claims.claim: Latrunculin-A treatment reduced N-Cadherin at AJs.
claims.source: This treatment depleted apical microtubules (Figure 3F", G", J) and consistent with this also reduced N-Cadherin at AJs (Figure 3F', G') and quantified in Figure 3I, I'.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and quantification following drug treatment.

claims.claim: Actin depletion led to a decrease in apical end-foot size.
claims.source: Actin depletion additionally led to a decrease in apical end-foot size (Figure 3F''', G''', K).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of end-foot area measurements.

claims.claim: An intact actin cable is required for maintenance of apical microtubule structures in neuroepithelial cells.
claims.source: These findings indicate that an intact actin cable is required for maintenance of apical microtubule structures as well as AJs in neuroepithelial cells and that the actin cytoskeleton serves to define apical end-foot dimensions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the latrunculin-A experiments.

claims.claim: The actin cytoskeleton serves to define apical end-foot dimensions.
claims.source: These findings indicate that an intact actin cable is required for maintenance of apical microtubule structures as well as AJs in neuroepithelial cells and that the actin cytoskeleton serves to define apical end-foot dimensions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the latrunculin-A experiments showing reduced end-foot size.

claims.claim: Microtubule growing tips emanate towards and along the constricted actin cable in delaminating cells.
claims.source: To assess the apical cytoskeletal configuration in delaminating cells, we next monitored EB3-GFP and F-tractin-mKate2 in cells with a small apical end-foot diameter (typically 1–2.5 μm), characteristic of delaminating cells (Figure 4A, Figure 4—video 1, 6 cells in 4 explants from 4 embryos). This revealed that microtubule growing tips still emanated towards and along the now constricted actin cable in such cells.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging of delaminating cells.

claims.claim: Microtubules remain closely associated with peripherally located actin in delaminating cells despite declining N-Cadherin.
claims.source: This suggests that despite declining N-Cadherin in delaminating cells microtubules remain closely associated with peripherally located actin.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that microtubules still associate with actin in cells with small end-feet.

claims.claim: Actin and microtubules form a composite tunnel-like configuration in delaminating cells.
claims.source: To elucidate further the spatial organisation of the cytoskeleton in delaminating cells, we used Stimulated Emission Depletion (STED) microscopy to generate super-resolution images of cells expressing F-tractin-mKate2 and EMTB-GFP (along with the neuronal differentiation gene Neurog2, as above). This revealed a close sub-apical alignment of actin and microtubules in such cells and, observed in 3-dimensions, these two cytoskeletal components appeared to form a composite tunnel-like configuration (Figure 4B, Figure 4—video 2, 4 cells from 2 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by STED microscopy of delaminating cells.

claims.claim: The prominent sub-apical EMTB-GFP labelling was highly dynamic and its intensity progressively increased as delamination proceeded.
claims.source: We monitored cells with moderate levels of EMTB-GFP transfection and observed that the prominent sub-apical EMTB-GFP labelling was highly dynamic and its intensity progressively increased as delamination proceeded.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging of cells undergoing delamination.

claims.claim: Following completion of abscission, the condensed band of EMTB-GFP was rapidly lost from the tip of the withdrawing cell-process.
claims.source: Following completion of abscission, the condensed band of EMTB-GFP was then rapidly lost from the tip of the withdrawing cell-process (Figure 4C, Figure 4—video 3, 22 cells in 15 slices; in each experiment slices are taken from 2 or 3 embryos, this applies here and in all similar experiments below).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging of cells undergoing delamination.

claims.claim: In control DMSO treated slices 19/61 cells (31%) abscised within 4 hr.
claims.source: In control DMSO treated slices 19/61 cells (31% in 29 slices) then abscised within 4 hr (Figure 5A; Figure 5—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a quantification from live imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Fewer labelled cells exposed to nocodazole delaminated during a 4 hr period (8/51 cells, 16%).
claims.source: However, fewer labelled cells exposed to nocodazole delaminated during this period (8/51 cells, 16% in 35 slices) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—video 2)(an effective nocodazole concentration (8.5 μM) for this embryo slice culture assay was determined by monitoring mitotic arrest see Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—videos 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is a quantification from live imaging experiments with nocodazole treatment.

claims.claim: Microtubules are required for delamination.
claims.source: These data suggest that microtubules are required for delamination.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the nocodazole experiments showing reduced delamination.

claims.claim: Many cells abscised in DMSO treated slices within 6 hr (24/55 cells, 44%).
claims.source: Cells were transfected as above and cell behaviour monitored following exposure to control DMSO or taxol. While many cells abscised in DMSO treated slices within 6 hr (24/55 cells, 44% in 23 slices), fewer cells cultured in the presence of taxol exhibited this behaviour (13/51 cells, 25% in 26 slices) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—video 6).
claims.evidence: This is a quantification from live imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Fewer cells cultured in the presence of taxol abscised within 6 hr (13/51 cells, 25%).
claims.source: Cells were transfected as above and cell behaviour monitored following exposure to control DMSO or taxol. While many cells abscised in DMSO treated slices within 6 hr (24/55 cells, 44% in 23 slices), fewer cells cultured in the presence of taxol exhibited this behaviour (13/51 cells, 25% in 26 slices) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—video 6).
claims.evidence: This is a quantification from live imaging experiments with taxol treatment.

claims.claim: Few cells delaminated in the presence of Stathmin-GFP (3/11 cells, 27%).
claims.source: Cells transfected with Stathmin-GFP and pCIG-Neurog2-NLS were monitored for 12–15 hr and delamination was quantified in cells poised to abscise. We found that few cells delaminated in the presence of Stathmin-GFP (3/11 cells, 27% in 6 slices, 5 experiments) (Figure 5—video 7), while many more cells underwent this step when only the vector control EGFP was expressed (10/17 cells, 59%, in 9 slices, 6 experiments) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B) (Figure 5—video 8).
claims.evidence: This is a quantification from live imaging experiments with Stathmin overexpression.

claims.claim: Many more cells underwent delamination when only the vector control EGFP was expressed (10/17 cells, 59%).
claims.source: We found that few cells delaminated in the presence of Stathmin-GFP (3/11 cells, 27% in 6 slices, 5 experiments) (Figure 5—video 7), while many more cells underwent this step when only the vector control EGFP was expressed (10/17 cells, 59%, in 9 slices, 6 experiments) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B) (Figure 5—video 8).
claims.evidence: This is a quantification from live imaging experiments with control vector.

claims.claim: Microtubule turnover and active growth are required for neuronal delamination.
claims.source: These data indicate that microtubules and their turnover and active growth are required for neuronal delamination.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the taxol and Stathmin experiments.

claims.claim: Sub-apical actin and microtubules accumulated in and were closely associated at the abscission site until final abscission.
claims.source: To confirm that the association between microtubules and actin continues throughout abscission, we performed further live imaging of cells co-transfected with F-tractin-td-Tomato, EMTB-GFP and pCIG-Neurog2. We again observed that sub-apical actin and microtubules accumulated in and were closely associated at the abscission site and that this remained until final abscission, following which both actin and microtubules were rapidly depleted from the cell-process tip (Figure 6A, Figure 6—video 1, 12 cells in 6 slices from 5 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with dual markers.

claims.claim: Following final abscission, both actin and microtubules were rapidly depleted from the cell-process tip.
claims.source: We again observed that sub-apical actin and microtubules accumulated in and were closely associated at the abscission site and that this remained until final abscission, following which both actin and microtubules were rapidly depleted from the cell-process tip (Figure 6A, Figure 6—video 1, 12 cells in 6 slices from 5 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with dual markers.

claims.claim: Taxol treatment blocked EMTB-GFP accumulation and subsequent detachment from the apical surface.
claims.source: To investigate the potential regulatory interactions between actin and microtubules, we next used taxol to stabilise microtubules in cells expressing mKate2-GPI, pCIG-Neurog2 and EMTB-GFP that were poised to delaminate. This confirmed cessation of EMTB-GFP accumulation and subsequent failure to detach from the apical surface.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with taxol treatment.

claims.claim: Taxol treatment interfered with stable accumulation of actin at the presumptive abscission site.
claims.source: We then monitored overall actin dynamics in cells expressing GFP-GPI, pCIG-Neurog2 and F-tractin-mKate2 that were poised to delaminate. We observed that while some cells in taxol-treated slices exhibited sub-apical constriction as judged by local cell shape change (Figure 6C white arrowheads,16/34 cells in 21 slices), this dynamic of sub-apical actin accumulation and subsequent loss ceased as indicated by fluorescence intensity measurements and such cells remained attached at the ventricular surface (Figure 6C, quantified in C'' (grey dashed line), Figure 6—video 4, 20 cells in 16 slices).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging and quantification with taxol treatment.

claims.claim: Blocking microtubule growth with taxol reduced cell delamination.
claims.source: It is interesting that blocking microtubule growth with taxol, while not abolishing acto-myosin contractility, interferes with stable accumulation of actin and that this correlates with reduced cell delamination.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the taxol experiments.

claims.claim: ML-7 treatment blocked sub-apical EMTB-GFP accumulation and loss in cells poised to delaminate.
claims.source: We then carried out the converse experiment, in which cells expressing mKate2-GPI, pCIG-Neurog2 and EMTB-GFP that were poised to delaminate were cultured in medium containing 20 μM ML-7 to inhibit acto-myosin constriction (Saitoh et al., 1987). We observed that the majority of the EMTB-GFP electroporated cells were now unable to initiate sub-apical constrictions (19/25 cells in 18 slices) and progress through to abscission, and that sub-apical EMTB-GFP labelling no longer exhibited its characteristic pattern of accumulation followed by loss.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with ML-7 treatment.

claims.claim: Microtubule and actin conformational dynamics are inter-dependent during delamination.
claims.source: These findings indicate that microtubule and actin conformational dynamics are inter-dependent; loss of actively growing microtubules blocked stable accumulation of actin at the presumptive abscission site and loss of acto-myosin activity abolished enrichment of microtubules at this location.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the taxol and ML-7 experiments.

claims.claim: Loss of actively growing microtubules blocked stable accumulation of actin at the presumptive abscission site.
claims.source: These findings indicate that microtubule and actin conformational dynamics are inter-dependent; loss of actively growing microtubules blocked stable accumulation of actin at the presumptive abscission site and loss of acto-myosin activity abolished enrichment of microtubules at this location.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the taxol experiments.

claims.claim: Loss of acto-myosin activity abolished enrichment of microtubules at the abscission site.
claims.source: These findings indicate that microtubule and actin conformational dynamics are inter-dependent; loss of actively growing microtubules blocked stable accumulation of actin at the presumptive abscission site and loss of acto-myosin activity abolished enrichment of microtubules at this location.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the ML-7 experiments.

claims.claim: Inhibition of either acto-myosin or microtubule activity reduced the incidence of neuronal delamination.
claims.source: Consistent with this inter-dependence, inhibition of either acto-myosin (Das and Storey, 2014) or microtubule activity (Figure 5C) reduced the incidence of neuronal delamination.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the ML-7 and taxol experiments.

claims.claim: Endogenous Drebrin is localised in the apical end-foot of neuroepithelial cells.
claims.source: To address whether Drebrin is a candidate mediator for actin-microtubule interaction during neuronal delamination we first assessed localisation of endogenous protein using IHC in transverse sections of the neural tube (Figure 7A). We found widespread cytoplasmic localisation of endogenous Drebrin, including in the apical end-foot (Figure 7A–A''', 3 sections from each of 4 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry.

claims.claim: Drebrin-mCherry co-localises with the actin belt and the apical EMTB-GFP-labelled microtubules.
claims.source: To look more closely at Drebrin localisation in end-feet we mis-expressed Drebrin-mCherry and EMTB-GFP and stained for actin in individual cells (Figure 7B–B'', 18 cells, 6 embryos). This analysis confirmed cytoplasmic localisation but also revealed co-localisation with the actin belt and the apical EMTB-GFP-labelled microtubules, quantified by measuring fluorescence intensities across the actin cable in a subset of cells (Figure 7C, 7 cells, 3 embryos, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by mis-expression and immunofluorescence.

claims.claim: Drebrin-YFP co-localises with actin in en face images.
claims.source: Similar co-localisation of Drebrin-YFP and actin was also apparent in en face images (Figures 7D, 5 explants from 5 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by mis-expression and immunofluorescence in en face orientation.

claims.claim: Drebrin is involved in the coordination of actin and microtubule dynamics during neuronal delamination.
claims.source: These localisation studies support the possibility that Drebrin is involved in the coordination of actin and microtubule dynamics during neuronal delamination
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the localization data.

claims.claim: Drebrin knockdown led to a marked reduction in the number of delaminating cells (4/27 cells, 15%).
claims.source: To test the requirement for Drebrin in this process, we next mis-expressed a Drebrin short-hairpin (Sh) construct (Dun et al., 2012) in the developing neural tube along with Neurog2. This led to a marked reduction in the number of delaminating cells (4/27 cells in 12–15 hr, 15% in 9 slices) compared to the scrambled GFP control (7/10 cells in 12–15 hr, 70% in 7 slices) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—videos 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with Drebrin knockdown.

claims.claim: Scrambled control cells delaminated at a higher rate (7/10 cells, 70%).
claims.source: This led to a marked reduction in the number of delaminating cells (4/27 cells in 12–15 hr, 15% in 9 slices) compared to the scrambled GFP control (7/10 cells in 12–15 hr, 70% in 7 slices) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—videos 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with scrambled control.

claims.claim: Drebrin is required for neuronal delamination.
claims.source: This requirement for Drebrin during neuronal delamination is consistent with a role for this protein in regulating cytoskeletal dynamics during this process and supports the possibility that Drebrin acts here as a link between actin-microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Apical abscission is characterised by dis-assembly of the centrosome-primary cilium complex followed by basal translocation of the centrosome.
claims.source: Apical abscission is characterised by dis-assembly of the centrosome-primary cilium complex which is followed by a basal translocation of the centrosome and so its retention in the withdrawing cell-process (Das and Storey, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: Differentiating neurons first constrict their sub-apical membranes and this is followed by basal translocation of the centrosome.
claims.source: To investigate the relationship between this translocation and the sub-apical constriction, neural tube cells were transfected with GFP-GPI, pCIG-Neurog2 and PACT-TagRFP, which labels centrosomes and cells were then subjected to live imaging. We observed that differentiating neurons first constricted their sub-apical membranes and that this was then strikingly followed by basal translocation of the centrosome.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging.

claims.claim: Centrosome translocation takes place late in the delamination process.
claims.source: This event therefore takes place late in the delamination process; indeed in some cells this movement was visible within a thinned membrane bridge between the withdrawing cell-process and the abscising particle (Figure 8A, Figure 8—video 1, 10 cells, 9 slices in 9 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging.

claims.claim: The translocating centrosome moves basally before the resolution of the sub-apical microtubules.
claims.source: Monitoring centrosome translocation in cells expressing PACT-TagRFP and EMTB-GFP further revealed that the translocating centrosome moves basally before the resolution of the sub-apical microtubules (Figure 8B, Figure 8—video 2, 8 cells in 8 slices and see Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with dual markers.

claims.claim: The centrosome passes through the sub-apical actin/microtubule tunnel-like configuration.
claims.source: This suggests that it passes through the sub-apical actin/microtubule tunnel-like configuration that we observed in cells poised to delaminate (Figure 4B, Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the timing of centrosome translocation relative to microtubule resolution.

claims.claim: The average diameter of the ring formed by rim microtubules is 0.89 ± 0.18 μm.
claims.source: To investigate this possibility further, we measured the diameter of the ring formed by rim microtubules visualised with acetylated alpha tubulin (17 cells in 2 explants from 2 embryos, Figure 8—figure supplement 1). This gave an average diameter of 0.89 ± 0.18 μm with an average centrosome diameter measured with IFT88, at the base of the ciliary membrane, of 0.32 ± 0.06 μm (36 cells in 2 explants from 2 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is based on measurements from immunofluorescence images.

claims.claim: The average centrosome diameter measured with IFT88 is 0.32 ± 0.06 μm.
claims.source: This gave an average diameter of 0.89 ± 0.18 μm with an average centrosome diameter measured with IFT88, at the base of the ciliary membrane, of 0.32 ± 0.06 μm (36 cells in 2 explants from 2 embryos).
claims.evidence: This is based on measurements from immunofluorescence images.

claims.claim: Centrosomal γ-tubulin has an average size of 0.98 ± 0.12 μm.
claims.source: Measurement of centrosomal γ-tubulin (which includes peri-centriolar material) revealed an average size of 0.98 ± 0.12 (21 cells, data not shown), consistent with centrosome size of 0.82 ± 0.17 μm in other contexts (Fu and Glover, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on measurements from immunofluorescence images and comparison to literature.

claims.claim: The centrosome moves through a tunnel-like cytoskeletal configuration formed by apical microtubules and the constricting actin cable.
claims.source: These data therefore support the possibility that the centrosome moves through a tunnel-like cytoskeletal configuration formed by apical microtubules and the constricting actin cable.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the size measurements and observations of centrosome translocation.

claims.claim: ML-7 treatment blocked centrosome translocation and delamination (5/31 cells).
claims.source: To test this, we observed cells in slices transfected with GFP-GPI, pCIG-Neurog2 and PACT-TagRFP that were cultured in medium containing ML-7, to block acto-myosin constriction. In such conditions, few cells delaminated and exhibited sub-apical constrictions or centrosome translocation within 6 hr (Figure 8C, Figure 8—video 3, 5/31 cells in 9 slices).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with ML-7 treatment.

claims.claim: Taxol treatment blocked centrosome translocation and delamination (4/24 cells).
claims.source: To determine whether centrosome translocation also required active microtubules, slices transfected with the same constructs were exposed to 10 µM taxol, and again fewer cells exhibited centrosome translocation and abscised within 6 hr (Figure 8D, Figure 8—video 4, 4/24 cells in 12 slices) compared with DMSO control conditions (Figure 8E, Figure 8—video 5, 9/26 cells in 14 slices).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with taxol treatment.

claims.claim: DMSO control cells exhibited centrosome translocation and delamination (9/26 cells).
claims.source: To determine whether centrosome translocation also required active microtubules, slices transfected with the same constructs were exposed to 10 µM taxol, and again fewer cells exhibited centrosome translocation and abscised within 6 hr (Figure 8D, Figure 8—video 4, 4/24 cells in 12 slices) compared with DMSO control conditions (Figure 8E, Figure 8—video 5, 9/26 cells in 14 slices).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging with DMSO control.

results.result: The authors identify a conserved wheel-like microtubule organization in neuroepithelial cells, composed of centrosome-nucleated radial and rim microtubules that align with the apical actin cable and adherens junctions. This configuration is observed in both chick and mouse spinal cord and cortex, with microtubules radiating from the centrosome and bending to run along the actin cable at the cell periphery.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C51-C61, C122, C123, C132, and C136 collectively demonstrate the wheel-like microtubule architecture through multiple complementary approaches: fixed immunofluorescence (C51-C57), live imaging with EB3-GFP tracking (C58-C61), super-resolution microscopy (C4, C5), and cross-species validation in mouse (C54, C55). The quantitative measurements (C52: 2.57 ± 0.5 μm diameter, C56: 71% co-alignment) and dynamic tracking data (C60, C61) provide strong converging evidence. Sample sizes are adequate (21-95 cells across multiple embryos) and the conservation across species strengthens the findings.

results.result: Microtubules maintain adherens junctions in neuroepithelial cells. Nocodazole treatment for 1 hour depleted apical microtubules and significantly reduced N-Cadherin at adherens junctions, while not affecting actin levels at the adhesion belt or apical end-foot area.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C62, C63, C125, and C147 are well-supported by the nocodazole experiments with appropriate controls (DMSO), quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements (C63: p<0.0001), and adequate sample sizes (276-304 measurements across 3 experiments). The specificity of the effect (microtubules and N-Cadherin reduced, but not actin at belt or end-foot area) strengthens the conclusion. The 1-hour timeframe is appropriate for assessing acute effects.

results.result: Actin maintains microtubules, adherens junctions, and apical end-foot dimensions in neuroepithelial cells. Latrunculin-A treatment for 15 minutes dramatically reduced apical actin, depleted apical microtubules, reduced N-Cadherin at adherens junctions, and decreased apical end-foot size.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C67-C72, C124, C148, and C149 are supported by latrunculin-A experiments with appropriate controls, quantitative measurements (C69, C70: p<0.0001), and adequate sample sizes (222-334 measurements across 2-3 experiments). The comprehensive effects on multiple cellular components (actin, microtubules, N-Cadherin, end-foot size) demonstrate the central role of actin. The 15-minute timeframe is appropriate for acute actin depletion. The asymmetry with nocodazole effects (which didn't affect end-foot size) strengthens the specificity of actin's role.

results.result: During neuronal delamination, microtubules and actin form a tunnel-like configuration at the abscission site. Live imaging shows microtubule growing tips emanate toward the constricted actin cable in delaminating cells, and STED microscopy reveals a composite tunnel-like structure. EMTB-GFP intensity progressively increases during delamination and is rapidly lost after abscission.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 and C126 are supported by complementary imaging approaches: live imaging with EB3-GFP and F-tractin-mKate2 (C73, C74), STED super-resolution microscopy (C75), and time-lapse EMTB-GFP imaging (C76, C77). The sample sizes are adequate (6 cells for live imaging, 4 cells for STED, 22 cells for EMTB-GFP dynamics). The tunnel-like configuration is directly visualized in 3D with STED (C75), and the dynamic changes are documented with appropriate temporal resolution.

results.result: Microtubules and their dynamic turnover are required for neuronal delamination. Nocodazole treatment reduced delamination from 31% to 16%, taxol treatment reduced it from 44% to 25%, and Stathmin-GFP overexpression reduced it from 59% to 27%.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C85 are supported by three independent pharmacological/genetic approaches with appropriate controls (DMSO for drugs, EGFP for Stathmin). Sample sizes are adequate (51-61 cells for nocodazole, 51-55 cells for taxol, 11-17 cells for Stathmin). The convergence of evidence from microtubule depolymerization (nocodazole), stabilization (taxol), and sequestration of tubulin (Stathmin) strongly supports the requirement for dynamic microtubules. However, statistical significance is not explicitly stated, which is a minor limitation.

results.result: Actin and microtubule dynamics are inter-dependent during delamination. Taxol treatment blocked EMTB-GFP accumulation and interfered with stable actin accumulation at the abscission site. ML-7 treatment blocked sub-apical EMTB-GFP accumulation. Inhibition of either acto-myosin or microtubule activity reduced delamination.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C95, C127, and C128 are supported by reciprocal perturbation experiments with dual-marker live imaging (F-tractin-td-Tomato and EMTB-GFP). The taxol experiments (C88, C89, C93) and ML-7 experiments (C91, C94) demonstrate bidirectional regulation. Quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements over time with 2-way ANOVA (p<0.001 for taxol, p=0.002 for ML-7) provide statistical support. Sample sizes are adequate (12-20 cells per condition). The inter-dependence is further supported by the observation that both treatments reduce delamination (C95).

results.result: Drebrin is a potential coordinator of actin and microtubule dynamics during delamination. Endogenous Drebrin localizes to the apical end-foot and co-localizes with the actin belt and apical microtubules. Drebrin knockdown reduced delamination from 70% to 15%.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C102, C12, C138, and C139 are supported by localization studies (immunohistochemistry and mis-expression with quantification) and functional knockdown experiments. The localization data (C96-C98) with adequate sample sizes (18 cells for mis-expression, 5 explants for en face) demonstrate Drebrin's position to mediate actin-microtubule interactions. The knockdown experiment (C100, C101) shows a dramatic reduction in delamination (70% to 15%) with appropriate scrambled control. However, the claim that Drebrin is a 'coordinator' (C12, C99, C139) is somewhat inferential, as direct mechanistic evidence is limited to localization and requirement.

results.result: The centrosome translocates through a tunnel-like actin-microtubule configuration during delamination. Live imaging shows that differentiating neurons first constrict sub-apically, then the centrosome translocates basally late in the process, moving before resolution of sub-apical microtubules. Size measurements support the centrosome (0.98 ± 0.12 μm) passing through the microtubule ring (0.89 ± 0.18 μm).
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C103-C111 are supported by live imaging with PACT-TagRFP and EMTB-GFP (C104-C106) and quantitative size measurements (C108-C110). Sample sizes are adequate (10 cells for centrosome translocation, 17-36 cells for size measurements). The timing of centrosome translocation relative to microtubule resolution (C106) and the size compatibility (C108-C110) support the tunnel model (C107, C111). However, C107 and C111 are inferred rather than directly demonstrated, as the centrosome is not visualized passing through the tunnel in real-time with all three components (actin, microtubules, centrosome) simultaneously.

results.result: Centrosome translocation requires inter-dependent actin and microtubule activity. ML-7 treatment reduced centrosome translocation and delamination to 5/31 cells (16%), taxol treatment reduced it to 4/24 cells (17%), compared to 9/26 cells (35%) in DMSO control.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C112-C115 are supported by live imaging experiments with ML-7 and taxol treatments using PACT-TagRFP to track centrosomes. Sample sizes are adequate (24-31 cells per condition). The reduction in centrosome translocation with both acto-myosin inhibition (ML-7) and microtubule stabilization (taxol) demonstrates the requirement for both cytoskeletal systems. However, statistical significance is not explicitly stated, which is a limitation.

results.result: The centrosome is required for delamination. Chromophore-assisted light inactivation (CALI) targeting the centrosome with PACT-KillerRed compromised centrosomal proteins, reduced microtubule nucleation by 48%, and reduced delamination from 60% to 25%.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C116-C121 are supported by CALI experiments with appropriate controls (PACT-TagRFP). The validation experiments (C116, C117) demonstrate specificity of the CALI approach (5/5 cells showed effect with KillerRed, 25/25 cells showed no effect with TagRFP). The functional consequence on microtubule nucleation (C118: 48% reduction, 22 cells) and delamination (C119, C120: 60% to 25%, adequate sample sizes) provide strong evidence. The CALI approach is innovative and well-controlled.

results.result: Background claims establishing the importance of neuronal delamination, its defects (periventricular heterotopias), genetic basis, and prior knowledge about apical abscission, adherens junctions, microtubules, and the centrosome in neuroepithelial cells and neuronal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C14-C50 are primarily background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims establish the context and rationale for the study. They are well-supported by the cited references and represent accurate summaries of established knowledge in the field. These are not novel findings from this study but provide essential context.

results.result: Neuronal delamination is an active process that requires nucleation of apical microtubules and inter-dependent microtubule and actin dynamics. It is not sufficient to downregulate N-cadherin alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C129, C130, and C173 are summary conclusions supported by the collective evidence from the study. The requirement for active microtubule nucleation (C121), dynamic microtubules (C85), inter-dependent actin-microtubule dynamics (C92), and centrosome function (C13) all support the conclusion that delamination is an active process beyond N-cadherin downregulation. These are well-justified integrative conclusions from the experimental results.

results.result: Discussion claims comparing the findings to prior work in other cell types, proposing mechanisms, and speculating on broader implications. These include comparisons to kidney epithelial cells, myoblasts, cytokinesis, and discussions of potential molecular mechanisms involving Drebrin, RhoA, endocytosis, and centrosome function.
results.evaluation: Claims C131, C133-C135, C137, C140-C146, C150-C172 are primarily discussion points that compare the current findings to prior literature, propose mechanisms, or speculate on broader implications. Many are explicitly speculative (C140, C142, C156, C162, C169, C171, C172) or based on comparisons to other systems (C131-C135, C164-C168). While these are reasonable interpretations and hypotheses, they are not directly tested in this study and represent future directions rather than established results. They are appropriately presented as discussion points.
